guides.title: How a Computer Works: Bits, Logic Gates & the CPU
guides.summary: From a single on/off switch to a working processor: how bits and binary numbers, Boolean logic gates, adders and memory cells, and the fetch-decode-execute cycle combine to turn electricity into computation.

sections.heading: Bits, Bytes and Binary Numbers
sections.body: A computer stores and manipulates information as bits. A bit (binary digit) is the smallest unit of data and holds exactly one of two values, written 0 or 1. Physically a bit is a voltage level on a wire or the charge state of a tiny capacitor: conventionally a 'low' voltage (near 0 volts) means 0 and a 'high' voltage (e.g. ~1.0–3.3 V in modern chips) means 1. Bits are grouped: 8 bits = 1 byte, which can represent 2^8 = 256 distinct values (0–255). Numbers are stored in base-2 (binary) rather than base-10 (decimal). In base-2 each digit position is a power of two: reading right to left the place values are 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128. To convert binary to decimal, multiply each bit by its place value and sum. Example: binary 1011 = 1·8 + 0·4 + 1·2 + 1·1 = 11 decimal. To convert decimal to binary, repeatedly divide by 2 and read the remainders bottom-to-top: 13 ÷ 2 = 6 r1, 6 ÷ 2 = 3 r0, 3 ÷ 2 = 1 r1, 1 ÷ 2 = 0 r1 → 1101. Common groupings: a 'nibble' is 4 bits (one hexadecimal digit, 0–F); a 'word' on most modern CPUs is 32 or 64 bits. Storage prefixes: 1 kilobyte (KB) = 1000 bytes, 1 kibibyte (KiB) = 1024 bytes; the same distinction applies to MB/MiB and GB/GiB.

sections.heading: Boolean Logic and the Fundamental Gates
sections.body:
All computation reduces to Boolean algebra, invented by George Boole (1854), which operates on two values TRUE (1) and FALSE (0). A logic gate is a physical circuit (built from transistors) that computes one Boolean function of its inputs. The core gates and their rules:
• NOT (inverter): 1 input; output is the opposite. NOT 0 = 1, NOT 1 = 0.
• AND: output 1 only if ALL inputs are 1. 1 AND 1 = 1; everything else = 0.
• OR: output 1 if AT LEAST ONE input is 1. 0 OR 0 = 0; everything else = 1.
• XOR (exclusive OR): output 1 if inputs DIFFER. 1 XOR 0 = 1, 1 XOR 1 = 0. XOR is the heart of binary addition.
• NAND (NOT-AND) and NOR (NOT-OR): the negations of AND and OR. NAND is 'universal' — any other gate can be built from NAND gates alone, which is why chip factories optimize for it.
A truth table lists every input combination and the resulting output. For a 2-input gate there are 2^2 = 4 rows. Gates are the vocabulary of hardware; the entire CPU is millions to billions of these gates wired together.

sections.heading: From Gates to Arithmetic: the Adder
sections.body: To add two bits you need the sum bit and the carry bit. A 'half adder' does this with two gates: SUM = A XOR B, CARRY = A AND B. Check: 1 + 1 in binary is 10 (sum 0, carry 1) — XOR gives 0, AND gives 1. A 'full adder' also accepts a carry-in from the previous column, using two half adders plus an OR gate: SUM = A XOR B XOR Cin; Cout = (A AND B) OR (Cin AND (A XOR B)). Chaining n full adders side by side — feeding each stage's carry-out into the next stage's carry-in — produces a 'ripple-carry adder' that adds two n-bit numbers. This is literally how a CPU's arithmetic-logic unit (ALU) adds integers. Subtraction reuses the same adder via 'two's complement': to compute A − B, flip every bit of B (NOT) and add 1, then add to A. Multiplication is repeated shift-and-add; division is repeated subtract-and-shift. The key insight: with just AND, OR, XOR and NOT you can build every arithmetic operation a computer performs.

sections.heading: Remembering a Bit: Latches, Flip-Flops and Registers
sections.body: Gates alone are 'combinational' — outputs depend only on current inputs, with no memory. To store a value you use feedback. Cross-coupling two NOR gates (each gate's output feeds the other's input) creates an SR (Set-Reset) latch that holds a single bit indefinitely once set, because the loop keeps refreshing itself. Adding a clock input turns it into a D flip-flop, which captures its data input only on the rising edge of the clock signal and holds it until the next edge — this makes memory predictable and synchronized. A 'register' is a row of flip-flops (e.g. 64 of them) that stores one machine word; CPUs have a small set of named registers (like RAX, RBX on x86-64) used as ultra-fast scratchpads. Main memory (DRAM) instead stores each bit as charge on a tiny capacitor, which leaks and must be 'refreshed' thousands of times per second — that is why it is called Dynamic RAM. The trade-off across the whole machine is speed versus capacity: flip-flop registers are fastest but few; DRAM is slower but vast.

sections.heading: The CPU and the Fetch-Decode-Execute Cycle
sections.body:
The Central Processing Unit executes a program — a list of simple instructions stored in memory — by repeating one loop billions of times per second:
1. FETCH: the Program Counter (PC) register holds the memory address of the next instruction. The CPU copies that instruction from memory into the Instruction Register.
2. DECODE: the control unit interprets the instruction's bit pattern (the 'opcode') to determine the operation and its operands — e.g. 'ADD register 1 to register 2'.
3. EXECUTE: the ALU or another unit performs the operation (add, compare, move data, jump).
4. WRITE-BACK / UPDATE: results are stored in a register or memory, and the PC advances to the next instruction (or is set to a new address by a jump/branch).
This is the von Neumann architecture (John von Neumann, 1945): program instructions and data live in the same memory. Instructions belong to the CPU's 'instruction set architecture' (ISA), such as x86-64, ARM, or RISC-V. Modern CPUs speed this up with pipelining (working on several instructions' stages at once, like an assembly line), multiple cores (independent CPUs on one chip), and caches.

sections.heading: Buses, the Memory Hierarchy and the Clock
sections.body:
Components communicate over 'buses' — shared bundles of wires. The address bus carries which memory location to access, the data bus carries the actual bits, and the control bus carries signals like read/write. Because fast memory is expensive, computers use a hierarchy, fastest and smallest at the top:
• CPU registers — ~1 KB total, access ~1 clock cycle.
• L1 cache — tens of KB, ~1–4 cycles.
• L2/L3 cache — hundreds of KB to tens of MB, ~10–40 cycles.
• Main memory (DRAM) — many GB, ~100–300 cycles.
• SSD/hard disk (persistent storage) — hundreds of GB to TB, thousands to millions of cycles.
Everything is paced by the clock, a crystal oscillator emitting a square wave. A 3 GHz clock ticks 3 billion times per second (each tick is ~0.33 nanoseconds). On each tick the synchronized flip-flops latch their new values, so the clock is the metronome that keeps billions of gates working in lockstep.

sections.heading: Worked Example: Adding 5 + 3 Inside the Machine
sections.body:
Suppose a program says 'load 5, load 3, add, store the result.' Trace it:
1. Decimal 5 becomes binary 0101; decimal 3 becomes 0011.
2. FETCH/DECODE: the CPU reads a 'load' instruction, decodes it, and copies 0101 into register R1, then 0011 into register R2.
3. EXECUTE (ADD): the 4-bit ripple adder processes column by column, right to left, using full-adder rules SUM = A XOR B XOR Cin:
   • Column 1: 1 + 1 = sum 0, carry 1.
   • Column 2: 0 + 1 + carry 1 = sum 0, carry 1.
   • Column 3: 1 + 0 + carry 1 = sum 0, carry 1.
   • Column 4: 0 + 0 + carry 1 = sum 1, carry 0.
   Reading the sum bits gives 1000 = decimal 8. Correct.
4. WRITE-BACK: 1000 is stored back to a register or memory, and the PC advances. The whole sequence completes in a handful of clock cycles — well under a billionth of a second. Nothing in this chain is magic: it is only voltages, gates and a clock repeating the same disciplined loop.

sections.heading: Common Misconceptions and Practical Notes
sections.body:
• 'Computers understand code.' They do not — a CPU only responds to bit patterns. Programming languages are translated (compiled or interpreted) down to those machine instructions.
• 'More gigahertz always means faster.' Clock speed is only one factor; instructions-per-cycle, core count, cache size, and memory speed often matter more. A 3 GHz modern chip vastly outperforms an old 3 GHz chip.
• 'RAM and storage are the same thing.' RAM (DRAM) is fast, volatile working memory that clears on power-off; storage (SSD/disk) is slower but persistent. Programs run in RAM but are saved to storage.
• 'A bit can be 0, 1, or empty.' A bit is always exactly one of two states; there is no third 'blank.'
Practical notes: overheating throttles clock speed, so cooling matters; error-correcting-code (ECC) memory adds extra bits to detect and fix bit-flips (important for servers); and the same binary logic scales from a $1 microcontroller to a supercomputer — only the number of gates and cores changes. Understanding this bottom layer demystifies everything above it, from operating systems to apps.

sections.heading: Transistors: The Physical Switch Behind Every Gate
sections.body:
Every AND, OR and NOT gate described so far is an abstraction sitting on top of a physical device: the transistor. Modern chips are built from the MOSFET (metal-oxide-semiconductor field-effect transistor), a three-terminal switch with a source, a drain and a gate. Apply a high enough voltage to the gate and an electric field opens a conducting channel between source and drain, letting current flow — the transistor turns 'on.' Drop the gate voltage below a threshold and the channel pinches off — it turns 'off.' That is the entire physical basis of the 1s and 0s from earlier in this guide: a voltage near the supply rail counts as a logical 1, a voltage near ground counts as a logical 0, and the transistor is simply a voltage-controlled valve deciding which one you get.

Real circuits pair two flavors of this switch: an NMOS transistor that conducts when its gate is HIGH, and a PMOS transistor that conducts when its gate is LOW. Wiring one of each so they're never both on at once is called CMOS (complementary MOS) — the technology behind essentially every processor made since the 1980s. The complementary pairing means meaningful current only flows briefly during a switching transition, not while a gate sits idle at a steady 0 or 1, which is why CMOS chips run cool enough to fit in a phone rather than needing industrial cooling.

The transistor was invented at Bell Labs in December 1947 by John Bardeen, Walter Brattain and William Shockley (work that earned them the 1956 Nobel Prize in Physics), replacing the vacuum tube — a fragile, power-hungry glass bulb that did the same switching job at roughly a hundred times the size, with a lifespan measured in months. ENIAC, one of the first electronic general-purpose computers (1945), used about 17,468 vacuum tubes and needed technicians on standby because tubes failed constantly under continuous operation. Intel's 4004 (1971), the first commercial microprocessor, packed 2,300 transistors onto one chip; a modern laptop or phone processor packs many billions onto a chip smaller than a fingernail. That relentless doubling of transistor density roughly every two years is what Gordon Moore observed in 1965, and it is what the entire industry has spent sixty years chasing — every gate discussed earlier in this guide is, physically, just a handful of these switches.

sections.heading: Instruction Sets: How Software Becomes Electricity
sections.body:
The fetch-decode-execute cycle explains how a CPU processes one instruction, but it glosses over a crucial question: what does an instruction actually look like as bits? The answer is the instruction set architecture (ISA) — a fixed vocabulary of operations the CPU's decoder understands, and the contract every compiler and assembler must target. An instruction is itself just a binary number, sliced into fields: an opcode identifying the operation, and operand fields identifying which registers or memory addresses it acts on.

Take a simplified RISC-V instruction — RISC-V being an open, royalty-free ISA used in embedded chips and increasingly in laptops. Its base instructions are a fixed 32 bits wide. An 'add' instruction (add rd, rs1, rs2 — 'put rs1+rs2 into rd') is encoded as a 7-bit opcode field, a 5-bit destination-register field, a 3-bit function code, two 5-bit source-register fields, and a 7-bit function-extension field, all packed into that single 32-bit word. When this word arrives at the control unit during the decode stage, hard-wired logic reads those bit fields and raises exactly the control signals needed to route the two named registers into the ALU's adder inputs and steer the sum back into the destination register — the abstraction of an 'instruction' cashes out as specific wires going high or low.

Contrast this with x86-64, the ISA in most desktop and laptop processors, where instructions are variable-length — anywhere from 1 to 15 bytes — because x86 grew by accretion since 1978, layering new instructions onto an old design for backward compatibility rather than starting clean. This RISC (reduced, fixed-width, simple — RISC-V, ARM) versus CISC (complex, variable-width, feature-rich — x86) split is one of the enduring architecture debates in computing.

None of this is written by hand for large programs. A compiler (for C or Rust) or a virtual machine (for Java or Python) translates human-readable source code down through several layers — typically first to assembly language, a human-readable one-to-one stand-in for machine instructions (mov, add, jmp and so on) — and an assembler then converts that into the raw opcodes the fetch-decode-execute cycle actually consumes. Every app on your phone, however sophisticated, bottoms out here: a stream of 32- or 64-bit words the decoder splits into opcode and operand fields, over and over, billions of times a second.

sections.heading: Equipment You'll Actually Need
sections.body: None of this requires a professional lab — a basic hobby-electronics setup is enough to build and test real logic gates with your own hands, not just simulate them.
ingredients: A solderless breadboard (an inexpensive reusable prototyping board, sold at any electronics/hobby store)

A handful of basic logic-gate ICs from the 7400-series (e.g. a 7408 AND, 7432 OR, 7404 NOT, 7486 XOR) or the 74HC00-series CMOS equivalents — sold individually and cheaply at any electronics/hobby store
Assorted jumper wires (male-to-male breadboard wires, sold in packs)
A simple 5V power source — a small benchtop power supply, or a battery pack (e.g. 4 AA batteries in a holder) with a basic voltage regulator or current-limiting resistor
A few 5mm LEDs plus matching 220-330 ohm resistors, wired as simple on/off output indicators
A digital multimeter (any basic $15-30 model with voltage and continuity testing) to verify what's actually happening at each pin
Optional: a free online logic-circuit simulator, useful for planning a circuit or checking your truth table before wiring anything physically

sections.heading: Step-by-Step: Build and Test a Half-Adder Yourself
sections.body: A half-adder — the same circuit worked through symbolically earlier in this guide — is small enough to breadboard in under an hour and gives you a real, physical demonstration that binary addition is nothing more than gates switching.
steps: Get one XOR gate IC and one AND gate IC (e.g. a 7486 and a 7408), each providing four independent 2-input gates per chip.
Check the chip's pinout diagram (printed on the packaging or easily looked up from the part number) and wire pin 14 to your +5V rail and pin 7 to ground on each chip.
Wire two jumper wires as inputs A and B, each switchable between +5V (logic 1) and ground (logic 0).
Feed A and B into both the first XOR gate's two inputs and the first AND gate's two inputs simultaneously (both chips read the same two input wires).
Connect the XOR gate's output through a 220-330 ohm resistor to an LED — this is your Sum output.
Connect the AND gate's output through a second resistor to a second LED — this is your Carry output.
Test all four input combinations in turn — (A=0,B=0), (0,1), (1,0), (1,1) — noting which LEDs light for each.
Compare your results against binary addition by hand: 0+0=00, 0+1=01, 1+0=01, 1+1=10 — the Sum LED should track the ones-place bit and the Carry LED the twos-place bit exactly.

Extension: wire a second half-adder plus an OR gate to combine their carry outputs, producing a full adder with a carry-in, and verify it correctly computes 1+1+1=11 (decimal 3) — the same block chained together seven more times becomes the 8-bit adder inside a real, simple CPU.

guides.title: Algorithms & Thinking Like a Programmer
guides.summary: What an algorithm is, how to measure its efficiency with Big-O notation, the core control structures and data structures, and a repeatable method for decomposing any problem into a correct, testable solution — with worked search and sort examples.

sections.heading: What an Algorithm Is
sections.body: An algorithm is a finite, precise sequence of unambiguous steps that transforms an input into a desired output, and that always terminates. The word comes from the 9th-century Persian mathematician al-Khwārizmī. Five formal properties define a good algorithm: (1) Finiteness — it stops after finitely many steps; (2) Definiteness — each step is exactly specified with no ambiguity; (3) Input — zero or more well-defined inputs; (4) Output — one or more outputs related to the input by a stated rule; (5) Effectiveness — each step is basic enough to be carried out exactly, in principle by hand. A recipe is a familiar analogy, but algorithms are stricter: 'add salt to taste' is too vague, whereas 'add 5 grams of salt' is definite. Correctness means the algorithm produces the right output for every valid input, which you argue by reasoning about a 'loop invariant' (a condition true before and after every iteration) or by mathematical induction. Determinism means the same input always yields the same output and the same steps; some algorithms are deliberately randomized (they use random choices) to gain speed or avoid worst cases.

sections.heading: Measuring Efficiency: Big-O Notation
sections.body:
Two correct algorithms can differ enormously in speed. We measure this abstractly with Big-O notation, which describes how the number of basic operations grows as the input size n grows, ignoring constant factors and hardware. Formally, an algorithm is O(f(n)) if, beyond some input size, its operation count is at most a constant times f(n). Common growth classes from best to worst:
• O(1) — constant: time independent of n (e.g. reading array element by index).
• O(log n) — logarithmic: halving the problem each step (binary search). For n = 1,000,000, log₂ n ≈ 20.
• O(n) — linear: one pass over the data.
• O(n log n) — the best possible for comparison sorting (mergesort, quicksort average).
• O(n²) — quadratic: nested loops over the data (bubble sort). For n = 1000 that is 1,000,000 operations.
• O(2ⁿ) and O(n!) — exponential/factorial: intractable beyond small n.
Worked contrast: with n = 1,000,000, an O(n) algorithm does ~10⁶ steps while an O(n²) one does ~10¹² — a million times more, the difference between milliseconds and days. We also distinguish best-, average-, and worst-case, and separately analyze 'space complexity' (memory used). Choosing a better algorithm usually beats any hardware upgrade.

sections.heading: The Four Building Blocks of Control Flow
sections.body:
Almost every algorithm is assembled from four constructs; the Böhm–Jacopini theorem (1966) proved that sequence, selection, and iteration alone can express any computable procedure.
• Sequence: steps executed one after another, top to bottom.
• Selection (branching): choose a path based on a condition — 'if temperature > 100 then boil, else wait.' Implemented with if / else if / else or switch statements.
• Iteration (looping): repeat steps while a condition holds ('while') or a fixed number of times ('for'). Every loop needs a clear termination condition or it runs forever (an 'infinite loop').
• Recursion: a function that calls itself on a smaller version of the problem, with a 'base case' that stops the recursion. Example — factorial: fact(n) = n · fact(n−1), base case fact(0) = 1. Recursion and iteration are interchangeable; recursion is elegant for naturally self-similar problems (trees, divide-and-conquer) but each call uses stack memory, so deep recursion can overflow the call stack.

sections.heading: Worked Example: Linear Search vs Binary Search
sections.body:
Task: find whether the number 37 is in a sorted list of 16 numbers.
Linear search checks each element left to right until found or exhausted — O(n), up to 16 comparisons here.
Binary search exploits sortedness by repeatedly halving the search range — O(log n), at most log₂ 16 = 4 comparisons:
1. Set low = 0, high = 15. Compute mid = (0+15)/2 = 7 (integer division). Compare list[7] to 37.
2. If list[7] < 37, the target must be in the right half: set low = mid + 1 = 8. If list[7] > 37, set high = mid − 1. If equal, done.
3. Repeat with the new low/high until low > high (not found) or a match is found.
For a list of 1,000,000 items, linear search may need 1,000,000 comparisons; binary search needs at most 20. Critical precondition: binary search REQUIRES the list to be sorted — running it on unsorted data gives wrong answers. Common bugs: forgetting mid = low + (high−low)/2 to avoid integer overflow, and off-by-one errors in updating low/high, which cause infinite loops or missed elements.

sections.heading: Worked Example: Bubble Sort vs Merge Sort
sections.body:
Sorting arranges data in order; the algorithm you choose determines whether a million-item sort takes a second or an hour.
Bubble sort (simple, O(n²)): repeatedly walk the list swapping any adjacent pair that is out of order; after each full pass the largest remaining element 'bubbles' to the end. Sorting [5, 1, 4, 2] ascending — pass 1 compares (5,1)→swap→[1,5,4,2], (5,4)→swap→[1,4,5,2], (5,2)→swap→[1,4,2,5]; pass 2 yields [1,2,4,5]. Easy to code but does up to n(n−1)/2 comparisons — for n=1000, about 500,000.
Merge sort (divide-and-conquer, O(n log n)): split the list in half repeatedly until each piece has one element (trivially sorted), then merge pairs back together in order by comparing their front elements. Merging [1,4] and [2,5] compares 1<2 → take 1, then 4>2 → take 2, then 4<5 → take 4, then 5 → [1,2,4,5]. Merge sort guarantees O(n log n) and is 'stable' (equal elements keep their order), at the cost of extra memory for the merge buffers. The lesson: the same task, radically different efficiency, depending on the algorithm's structure.

sections.heading: Data Structures: Choosing How to Store Information
sections.body:
The right data structure makes an algorithm simple and fast; the wrong one makes it slow or clumsy.
• Array: fixed-size, contiguous block; O(1) access by index, but inserting in the middle is O(n). Best when you know the size and access randomly.
• Linked list: nodes each pointing to the next; O(1) insert/delete at a known position, but O(n) to reach the k-th element. Good for frequent insertions/deletions.
• Stack (LIFO — last in, first out): push and pop from one end; models undo operations, function calls, expression evaluation.
• Queue (FIFO — first in, first out): add at back, remove from front; models task scheduling, printer buffers, breadth-first search.
• Hash table (map/dictionary): stores key→value pairs using a hash function to compute a storage slot; average O(1) lookup, insert and delete. The backbone of most fast lookups.
• Tree: hierarchical nodes with a root and children; a balanced binary search tree gives O(log n) search/insert/delete. Used for databases and file systems.
• Graph: nodes ('vertices') connected by edges; models networks, maps, and social connections, traversed with breadth-first or depth-first search.
Rule of thumb: pick the structure whose fast operations match what your algorithm does most often.

sections.heading: A Repeatable Problem-Solving Method
sections.body:
Thinking like a programmer is a disciplined process, not innate talent. Use this five-step loop for any problem:
1. UNDERSTAND: restate the problem in your own words; list the inputs, the required outputs, and the constraints. Write two or three concrete examples by hand, including edge cases (empty input, one item, largest allowed size, duplicates, negatives).
2. DECOMPOSE: break the big problem into smaller sub-problems you already know how to solve. Solving 'sort then binary-search' is two known pieces.
3. PLAN in pseudocode: write the logic in plain structured English before touching a real language — this separates thinking from syntax.
4. IMPLEMENT: translate the pseudocode to code, one small piece at a time, running it often.
5. TEST & DEBUG: run your hand-made examples, then edge cases. When it fails, use the scientific method — form a hypothesis about the bug, add print statements or a debugger to inspect variable values at each step, confirm or refute, and fix. Rubber-duck debugging (explaining your code line-by-line out loud) surfaces faulty assumptions surprisingly often.

sections.heading: Common Mistakes and Pitfalls
sections.body:
• Off-by-one errors: loops that run one iteration too many or too few, usually from confusing < with ≤ or mishandling zero-based indexing (the first element is index 0, the n-th is index n−1).
• Infinite loops: forgetting to change the loop variable so the exit condition is never met.
• Ignoring edge cases: code that works on typical input but crashes on empty lists, a single element, or the maximum size.
• Premature optimization: making code fast before making it correct and clear — first make it work, then measure with real data, then optimize the actual bottleneck.
• Integer overflow and division: assuming numbers can grow without limit, or that integer division 7/2 gives 3.5 (in most languages it gives 3, truncated).
• Not checking assumptions: e.g. running binary search on unsorted data, or assuming input is valid without validation.
• Copy-paste programming: duplicating logic instead of writing a reusable function, which multiplies bugs.
Good practice: write small, single-purpose functions; name variables meaningfully; test as you go; and always reason about correctness (does this hold for every input?) rather than trusting that one passing example proves the whole thing works.

sections.heading: Greedy Algorithms and Dynamic Programming: Two Higher-Level Strategies
sections.body:
Big-O tells you how an algorithm scales, but it says nothing about which strategy to reach for when designing one from scratch. Two of the most powerful general strategies sit above individual algorithms like sorting or searching: greedy algorithms and dynamic programming.

A greedy algorithm builds a solution one step at a time, always taking whatever choice looks best right now, and never reconsidering it. Making change is the classic illustration. With US coin denominations (1, 5, 10, 25 cents), greedily grabbing the largest coin that doesn't overshoot the target happens to always produce the fewest coins possible — 41 cents becomes 25+10+5+1, four coins, which is in fact optimal. But greedy is not a universally safe strategy: invent a currency with denominations {1, 3, 4} and ask for 6 cents. Greedy grabs a 4 first (the largest that fits), leaving 2, which it can only make as 1+1 — three coins total. The actual optimal answer is two coins (3+3). Greedy failed because this coin system lacks the 'greedy choice property' that US coins happen to have. The lesson generalizes: greedy algorithms are fast (often O(n log n) or better, since each choice is examined once) but require proof that local best choices never sabotage the global optimum — Dijkstra's shortest-path algorithm and Huffman coding are both greedy algorithms that happen to be provably correct.

Dynamic programming (DP) is what you reach for when greedy can't be proven safe but the problem has 'overlapping subproblems' — the same smaller calculation gets redone many times inside a naive recursive solution. The textbook demonstration is Fibonacci numbers: a naive recursive fib(n) = fib(n-1) + fib(n-2) recomputes the same smaller values from scratch inside both branches, and the total number of calls explodes to roughly 2^n — fib(40) alone triggers well over a billion redundant calls. DP fixes this by storing (memoizing) each subresult the first time it's computed and reusing it thereafter, collapsing the runtime from exponential to linear, O(n) — the difference between a program finishing instantly and one that's still running long after you've given up watching. The same idea, applied to two-dimensional problems, powers the 0/1 knapsack problem (choosing which items to pack into a weight-limited bag to maximize value), spell-checkers' 'did you mean' suggestions (via edit distance, formally the Levenshtein algorithm), and DNA sequence alignment in bioinformatics (the Needleman-Wunsch algorithm, 1970) — all built from the same core trick of never solving the same subproblem twice.

sections.heading: Recursion, the Call Stack, and When It Breaks
sections.body:
Recursion — a function calling itself — is one of the four building blocks of control flow, but treating it as 'just another loop' hides a real mechanical cost worth understanding directly. Every function call pushes a stack frame onto the call stack: a block of memory holding that call's local variables, its parameters, and the return address it needs to jump back to when it finishes. A recursive call doesn't avoid this — it pushes a brand-new frame every single time, even though it's 'the same function.'

Trace factorial(5) by hand: calling factorial(5) pushes a frame and, before it can return, calls factorial(4), which pushes its own frame and calls factorial(3), and so on down to factorial(0), the base case, which returns 1 immediately without recursing further. At that point five stack frames sit in memory simultaneously, each mid-execution, each waiting on the call below it. Only once factorial(0) returns does factorial(1) resume, multiply 1x1, and return 1 to factorial(2), which multiplies 2x1=2, and so on, unwinding back up to factorial(5), which finally computes 5x24=120. The stack grew to depth 5 and shrank back to 0 — memory a purely iterative loop, using one running total, would never have needed.

This has a hard consequence: recursion that goes too deep runs out of stack space and crashes with a stack overflow, not a graceful error. Python enforces an explicit recursion limit — 1,000 nested calls by default — specifically to convert what would otherwise be a memory-corrupting crash into a catchable exception. Forgetting a base case, or writing one that's never actually reached (a classic bug when the recursive step doesn't reliably move toward it), is the single most common way beginners trigger this. Some languages optimize a special case called tail recursion — where the recursive call is the very last thing the function does, with no pending work left afterward — by reusing the current stack frame instead of pushing a new one, but this is not universal: Python deliberately does not implement tail-call optimization, even for tail-recursive code, on the philosophy that stack traces should stay honest and readable. When recursion depth genuinely needs to scale with large input (traversing a very deep tree, say), the standard fix is to rewrite the algorithm iteratively using an explicit stack data structure you manage yourself on the heap, which has no such fixed limit.

sections.heading: Equipment You'll Actually Need
sections.body: This is one of the cheapest topics in the whole collection to practice hands-on — mostly you need time, paper, and a computer you probably already own.
ingredients: A computer with a free code editor or even a plain text editor installed
A free programming language interpreter — Python is the most common starting choice for algorithm practice and is freely downloadable, or already installed, on most systems
Pen and paper, or a whiteboard, for tracing an algorithm's execution step by step by hand before trusting it to a computer
A stopwatch, or simply the timing functions built into your chosen language, for measuring real runtime differences between algorithms

A deck of playing cards, genuinely useful for physically practicing sorting algorithms (spread a shuffled hand face-up and sort it using only bubble-sort-style adjacent swaps, then again by merge-sort-style splitting)
A stack of index cards or sticky notes, handy for modeling a call stack or a stack/queue data structure by hand

sections.heading: Step-by-Step: Trace and Time Three Sorting Algorithms Yourself
sections.body: Reading about Big-O is one thing; watching the gap between O(n squared) and O(n log n) open up on your own machine, in milliseconds you measured yourself, is what makes it stick.
steps: Write (or find and understand line-by-line) a working bubble sort function and a working merge sort function in your chosen language.

Pick 10 random two-digit numbers, write them on paper, and trace bubble sort by hand: repeatedly scan left to right swapping any adjacent out-of-order pair, and count exactly how many comparisons and swaps the full sort takes.
Trace merge sort by hand on the same 10 numbers: recursively split the list in half until each piece has one element, then merge pairs back together in sorted order, again counting comparisons.
Compare the two counts — bubble sort should take noticeably more comparisons even on this tiny list, and the gap only widens as the list grows.

Generate a random list of 5,000 numbers in code (most languages have a built-in random module) and time how long your bubble sort and merge sort each take, using the language's timing functions; record both numbers.
Repeat with 20,000 numbers (four times the size) and record the new times.
Compare the ratios: bubble sort's time should have grown roughly 16x (quadratically, matching O(n squared)) while merge sort's time grew only a bit more than 4x (matching O(n log n)).

Finally, time both algorithms on an already-sorted list of 20,000 numbers and then a reverse-sorted one, and notice bubble sort (with an early-exit flag added) finishes almost instantly on the sorted case but merge sort's time barely changes — a direct, hands-on demonstration of best-case versus worst-case behavior.

guides.title: Encoding, Data & Compression
guides.summary: How numbers, text, images and sound are all reduced to bits; Shannon's measure of information; how lossless and lossy compression shrink data; and how parity, checksums and error-correcting codes detect and repair the inevitable bit errors.

sections.heading: Representing Numbers: Integers, Negatives and Floats
sections.body: Everything in a computer is a pattern of bits; the meaning comes from the agreed encoding. Unsigned integers use plain binary: 8 bits represent 0 to 255 (2⁸−1). Negative numbers use 'two's complement': the leftmost bit is the sign, and a negative value is formed by inverting all bits of its magnitude and adding 1. In 8-bit two's complement, +5 is 00000101, and −5 is 11111011 (invert to 11111010, add 1). This clever scheme lets the same adder circuit handle addition and subtraction, and it represents −128 to +127. Real (fractional) numbers use floating-point, standardized as IEEE 754. A 32-bit 'single precision' float splits into 1 sign bit, 8 exponent bits, and 23 fraction ('mantissa') bits, encoding value = ±1.fraction × 2^(exponent−127). This is like scientific notation in binary and covers a vast range (~10^−38 to 10^38) but with limited precision — which is why 0.1 + 0.2 does not exactly equal 0.3 in most languages (0.1 has no exact binary representation, just as 1/3 has no exact decimal). Rule: never test floats for exact equality; compare within a small tolerance (epsilon).

sections.heading: Representing Text: ASCII, Unicode and UTF-8
sections.body: Text is stored by mapping each character to a number ('code point') and storing that number's bits. ASCII (1963) uses 7 bits to cover 128 characters — the English letters, digits, punctuation, and control codes. For example 'A' = 65 (1000001), 'a' = 97, '0' = 48, and space = 32; note letters are contiguous, so 'C' − 'A' = 2. ASCII cannot represent accented letters, non-Latin scripts, or emoji, so Unicode was created to assign a unique code point to every character in every writing system (over 149,000 characters as of recent versions), written U+XXXX in hexadecimal — e.g. U+00E9 is 'é', U+4E2D is '中', U+1F600 is a grinning face. UTF-8 is the dominant way to store Unicode as bytes: it uses 1 byte for the original ASCII characters (so ASCII files are valid UTF-8), 2 bytes for most European and Middle-Eastern scripts, 3 for most Asian scripts, and 4 for emoji and rare symbols. Its genius is backward compatibility and self-synchronization. Common bug: 'mojibake' — garbled text — happens when bytes encoded one way (say UTF-8) are decoded as another (say Latin-1); always store and declare the encoding explicitly.

sections.heading: Representing Images, Color and Sound
sections.body: A digital image is a grid of pixels, each storing a color. The most common color model is RGB: three numbers giving the intensity of Red, Green and Blue, usually 0–255 each (8 bits per channel = 24-bit 'true color', 16.7 million possible colors). Pure red is (255,0,0), white is (255,255,255), black is (0,0,0). A 1920×1080 image at 24 bits/pixel is 1920·1080·3 ≈ 6.2 million bytes uncompressed — hence the need for compression. A fourth 'alpha' channel adds transparency (RGBA, 32 bits). Sound is a continuous pressure wave that is 'sampled' — measured at regular intervals — turning it into numbers. CD audio uses a 44,100 Hz sample rate (44,100 measurements per second, per the Nyquist theorem, which says you must sample at least twice the highest frequency you want to capture; humans hear up to ~20,000 Hz) and 16 bits per sample, giving ~1.4 million bits per second for stereo. Every medium follows the same idea: convert a physical quantity into numbers, store the numbers as bits.

sections.heading: Information Theory: Entropy and the Limits of Compression
sections.body: Claude Shannon's 1948 information theory gives the mathematical foundation for compression. The 'information content' (surprise) of an event with probability p is I = −log₂(p) bits: a certain event (p = 1) carries 0 bits of information; a fair coin flip (p = 0.5) carries −log₂(0.5) = 1 bit. Entropy H is the average information per symbol from a source: H = −Σ pᵢ·log₂(pᵢ), summed over all symbols i, measured in bits per symbol. Entropy sets the theoretical minimum average number of bits needed to encode the source without loss — you cannot losslessly compress below the entropy. Worked example: a source emitting four symbols with probabilities 1/2, 1/4, 1/8, 1/8 has H = −(0.5·log₂0.5 + 0.25·log₂0.25 + 0.125·log₂0.125 + 0.125·log₂0.125) = 0.5·1 + 0.25·2 + 0.125·3 + 0.125·3 = 1.75 bits/symbol, so an ideal code averages 1.75 bits per symbol rather than the naive 2 bits. Compression works precisely because real data (English text, photos, sound) is far from random — it has structure and repetition, so its entropy is low and there is 'redundancy' to remove.

sections.heading: Lossless Compression: RLE and Huffman Coding
sections.body:
Lossless compression shrinks data so it can be perfectly reconstructed — essential for text, code, and archives. Two foundational methods:
• Run-Length Encoding (RLE): replace runs of identical values with a count and the value. 'AAAAAABBB' (9 bytes) becomes '6A3B' (4 bytes). Excellent for data with long runs (simple graphics, fax) but can make random data larger — hence it is rarely used alone.
• Huffman coding (David Huffman, 1952): assign short bit-codes to frequent symbols and long codes to rare ones, so the average is minimized. Build a binary tree bottom-up by repeatedly merging the two lowest-frequency nodes; the path from root to a leaf (left = 0, right = 1) is that symbol's code. Because no code is a prefix of another ('prefix-free'), the stream decodes unambiguously. Example — for the entropy source above, Huffman assigns codes 0, 10, 110, 111 (lengths 1, 2, 3, 3), exactly matching the 1.75-bit entropy. Real compressors like DEFLATE (used in ZIP, PNG, and gzip) combine a dictionary method with Huffman coding to approach the entropy limit.

sections.heading: Dictionary Methods and Lossy Compression
sections.body:
Dictionary (LZ) compression, from Lempel and Ziv (LZ77, 1977), replaces repeated sequences with a back-reference (a distance and length pointing to an earlier occurrence). In 'the cat sat on the mat', the second 'the ' becomes a pointer to the first. This is why text and code compress so well and underlies ZIP, gzip, and PNG. Lossy compression goes further by permanently discarding information humans barely perceive, achieving much smaller files:
• JPEG (photos): divides the image into 8×8 blocks, applies the Discrete Cosine Transform to express each block as frequencies, then coarsely rounds ('quantizes') the high-frequency detail the eye is insensitive to. A 'quality' setting controls how aggressively; too low produces blocky artifacts. JPEG can shrink a photo 10:1 with little visible loss.
• MP3/AAC (audio): use a 'psychoacoustic model' to drop sounds masked by louder nearby sounds, compressing music ~10:1.
• H.264/H.265 (video): additionally store only the differences between successive frames.
Golden rule: use lossless for anything you must reproduce exactly (text, source code, medical/legal images); use lossy only for perceptual media where small imperfections are acceptable, and never re-save lossy files repeatedly — each save degrades quality further ('generation loss').

sections.heading: Error Detection and Correction
sections.body:
Storage and transmission are imperfect: cosmic rays, electrical noise, and scratches flip bits. Codes add controlled redundancy so errors are caught or repaired.
• Parity bit: append one bit making the total number of 1s even (even parity). If a single bit flips, the count becomes odd and the error is detected — but not located, and two flips cancel out and go unnoticed. Detects any odd number of errors.
• Checksum / CRC (Cyclic Redundancy Check): compute a value from the data (CRC uses polynomial division) and send it alongside; the receiver recomputes and compares. CRC-32 reliably catches burst errors and is used in Ethernet, ZIP, and disk sectors.
• Hamming codes (Richard Hamming, 1950): place parity bits at power-of-two positions so their combination not only detects but pinpoints and corrects a single-bit error. A (7,4) Hamming code protects 4 data bits with 3 parity bits.
• ECC memory and RAID storage extend these ideas to fix errors automatically in servers and disk arrays.
Worked check: to send the 4 bits 1011 with even parity, count the 1s (three, odd), so the parity bit is 1, transmitting 10111. If the receiver gets 10101 (three 1s, odd) it knows something is wrong. Trade-off: more redundancy means stronger protection but larger data — engineers match the code strength to how noisy the channel is.

sections.heading: Real-World Formats: How ZIP, PNG, JPEG and MP3 Combine These Ideas
sections.body:
Nobody ships raw entropy calculations or a bare Huffman tree as a finished product — real file formats stack several of the techniques from this guide on top of each other, and knowing the stack explains a lot of everyday computing behavior that otherwise looks mysterious.

Take PNG, a lossless image format. Before compressing anything, PNG runs a filter pass over each row of pixels, replacing each pixel's stored value with the difference from a predicted value (often just the pixel to its left, or an average of neighbors) — because photographs and screenshots are usually smooth, most of these differences cluster near zero, which is exactly the low-entropy, repetitive data that compresses well. Only after this prediction step does PNG hand the result to DEFLATE, the same general-purpose algorithm used inside ZIP files, which combines LZ77-style dictionary matching (spotting repeated byte sequences and replacing them with a short back-reference) with Huffman coding on what's left over. That's why zipping an already-compressed JPEG barely shrinks it at all — DEFLATE is hunting for redundancy the JPEG encoder already squeezed out.

JPEG itself takes the lossy route. It splits an image into 8x8 pixel blocks and applies the discrete cosine transform (DCT) to each block, re-expressing the block's pixel values as a sum of cosine wave patterns of increasing spatial frequency. JPEG then quantizes (coarsens) the high-frequency coefficients much more aggressively than the low-frequency ones, because human vision is far less sensitive to fine high-frequency detail than to broad shifts in brightness and color — this is the actual lossy step, and it's tunable, which is what the 'quality' slider in an image editor controls. Whatever coefficients survive quantization are then run-length and Huffman coded, the same lossless finishing move as PNG. Because information is permanently discarded at quantization, repeatedly opening, editing and re-saving a JPEG accumulates fresh rounding loss each time — generation loss — which is why professional photo workflows edit from an uncompressed or losslessly-compressed master and only export to JPEG once, at the end.

MP3 audio applies the same lossy philosophy to sound using a psychoacoustic model instead of a visual one: it exploits auditory masking, the documented fact that a loud tone makes nearby quieter frequencies (and sounds immediately following it) inaudible to human ears even though they're still physically present in the waveform. MP3 encoders discard those masked components before Huffman-coding what remains, which is how a 128 kbps MP3 squeezes CD-quality audio (roughly 1,411 kbps uncompressed) down to about one-eleventh its original size while still sounding, to most listeners, close to the original.

sections.heading: Base64 and the Practical Problem of Moving Binary Data as Text
sections.body:
Every encoding scheme discussed so far assumes the receiving system can handle arbitrary binary bytes. In practice, huge swaths of the infrastructure the internet is built on — early email transport, URLs, JSON documents, XML — were designed to carry printable text only, and choke on or silently mangle raw bytes below 32 or above 126. Base64 exists to smuggle arbitrary binary data through these text-only pipes safely.

The trick is a change of base. Binary data is naturally grouped in 8-bit bytes; Base64 regroups the same bit stream into 6-bit chunks instead, because 2^6 = 64, and 64 characters is exactly enough to cover A-Z, a-z, 0-9, plus two extra symbols (conventionally + and /) while staying entirely within safe printable ASCII. Since 8 and 6 don't share a clean multiple until 24 bits, Base64 processes input three raw bytes at a time (3 x 8 = 24 bits), re-slicing that block into four 6-bit groups (4 x 6 = 24 bits) — three bytes in, four printable characters out.

Walk it through by hand on the word 'Cat': the three ASCII bytes are 0x43, 0x61, 0x74 — in binary, 01000011 01100001 01110100. Concatenated into one 24-bit stream and re-cut into four 6-bit groups: 010000 110110 000101 110100. Converted to decimal, that's 16, 54, 5, 52. Looking each index up in the Base64 alphabet (A=0...Z=25, a=26...z=51, 0=52...9=61, then + and /) gives Q, 2, F, 0 — so 'Cat' becomes the text string 'Q2F0'. Notice the output is four characters for three input bytes: Base64 reliably inflates data by exactly one-third, a real and often-forgotten storage and bandwidth cost. When the input length isn't a clean multiple of three bytes, the encoder pads the final group with one or two '=' characters so the decoder knows exactly how many trailing bits to discard.

This is not encryption or compression — it adds no secrecy (anyone can decode Base64 instantly) and makes data larger, not smaller. Its entire job is compatibility. It's why images embedded directly inside a webpage's HTML or CSS often appear as a long data: URI string, why email attachments are transmitted as blocks of Base64 text under the hood, and why the two halves of a JSON Web Token (used to carry login session data) are readable Base64 blobs rather than raw bytes — in every case, the underlying binary or JSON payload has been re-based purely so it survives a text-only channel intact.

sections.heading: Equipment You'll Actually Need
sections.body: Most of this you can do with software you likely already have; a couple of cheap physical props make the abstract ideas concrete.
ingredients: A computer with a plain text editor and, ideally, a free hex editor (or a terminal capable of a hex dump, which most operating systems include by default) for inspecting raw bytes directly
A free scripting language interpreter such as Python, which has built-in support for compression (gzip/zlib), Base64 and bit-level manipulation without installing anything extra
A calculator with a 'programmer' or binary/hex conversion mode (a free feature on most phone and desktop calculator apps), or paper for manual binary math
A basic image-editing program capable of exporting the same picture as BMP, PNG and JPEG (many free/built-in ones can), for direct side-by-side file-size comparison
A pack of playing cards or a pair of dice, useful for hand-generating genuinely random data to compare against structured, repetitive data when testing how well something compresses
Optional: a Unix-like terminal (built into Linux and macOS; addable on Windows) for using standard zip/gzip utilities and byte-inspection tools directly on real files

sections.heading: Step-by-Step: Encode, Compress and Measure Data by Hand
sections.body: The fastest way to trust that Huffman coding and Base64 really work is to run a short piece of data through each of them yourself, by hand, and check the arithmetic.
steps: Take the string 'ABRACADABRA' (11 characters) and count each letter's frequency: A=5, B=2, R=2, C=1, D=1.

Build a Huffman tree by hand: repeatedly take the two lowest-frequency nodes (starting with the two count-1 letters), merge them into a new node whose weight is their sum, and keep repeating until one tree remains.
Walk the finished tree to read off each letter's binary code (left branch = 0, right branch = 1, root to leaf), and write down the resulting code table.

Encode the full 11-letter string with your code table and count the total bits used; compare that against a fixed-width code (5 distinct symbols needs 3 bits each, i.e. 33 bits for 11 letters) and compute the percentage saved.

Save the same 11-character string in a plain text file, then compress that file with any zip utility, and compare the file sizes on disk — notice the saved space is far less impressive than your hand calculation, because ZIP's fixed header/metadata overhead dominates on such a tiny file, a real and common gotcha.

Pick a 3-letter word from your own name and hand-encode it in Base64 following the byte-splitting method described earlier, then check your answer with a scripting language's built-in Base64 function.

Save one photo as an uncompressed BMP, then export the same photo as a PNG and as a JPEG at medium quality from an image editor; record all three file sizes and compute each one's compression ratio relative to the BMP.

Zoom into the JPEG version at high magnification around a sharp edge in the image and look for faint square patterning — you're looking directly at the boundaries of the 8x8 blocks the DCT compression step operates on.

guides.title: Cryptography & Keeping Secrets
guides.summary: The science of protecting information: confidentiality, integrity and authentication; why classical ciphers fail; symmetric and public-key encryption with a worked RSA example; hashes, signatures and certificates; and the practical rules for storing passwords and managing keys safely.

sections.heading: The Four Goals and the Core Vocabulary
sections.body: Cryptography is the mathematical study of securing communication in the presence of adversaries. It aims at four distinct goals: (1) Confidentiality — only intended parties can read the message; (2) Integrity — the message has not been altered; (3) Authentication — the parties are who they claim to be; (4) Non-repudiation — a sender cannot later deny having sent a message. Key terms: 'plaintext' is the original readable message; 'ciphertext' is the scrambled result; 'encryption' converts plaintext to ciphertext; 'decryption' reverses it; a 'cipher' is the algorithm; and the 'key' is the secret parameter that controls the transformation. A crucial principle is Kerckhoffs's principle (1883): a system must remain secure even if everything about it except the key is public knowledge. This is why real cryptography uses openly published, peer-reviewed algorithms — 'security through obscurity' (hoping the enemy never learns your method) is fragile and discouraged. The security should rest entirely on keeping the key secret, and on the algorithm being mathematically hard to break.

sections.heading: Classical Ciphers and Why They Fail
sections.body:
Early ciphers illustrate the ideas and the pitfalls.
• Caesar cipher: shift each letter by a fixed amount. With shift 3, A→D, B→E, so 'HELLO' becomes 'KHOOR'. There are only 25 possible shifts, so an attacker simply tries them all ('brute force') in seconds.
• Substitution cipher: replace each letter by another via a fixed mapping. There are 26! ≈ 4×10²⁶ keys — too many to brute force — yet it still falls to 'frequency analysis': in English, E is the most common letter (~12.7%), then T, A, O; the most common ciphertext letter is probably E, and the pattern unravels.
• Vigenère cipher: use a repeating keyword to vary the shift per position, defeating simple frequency analysis for centuries — but the repetition of the key creates detectable patterns (the Kasiski examination and index of coincidence) that reveal the key length, after which each column is a Caesar cipher.
The lesson: an intuitively strong scheme can hide a fatal statistical weakness. Modern ciphers are designed so that ciphertext is statistically indistinguishable from random noise, defeating all such analysis. Never invent your own cipher for real use — use vetted standards.

sections.heading: Symmetric Encryption and the One-Time Pad
sections.body: Symmetric (secret-key) encryption uses the same key to encrypt and decrypt. The theoretically perfect cipher is the one-time pad: XOR each plaintext bit with a truly random key bit that is as long as the message, used only once. If the key is random, secret, and never reused, the ciphertext reveals nothing — provably unbreakable (Shannon proved this). Its impracticality is key distribution and the enormous key length, so real systems use block ciphers. The standard is AES (Advanced Encryption Standard, adopted 2001), which encrypts data in 128-bit blocks using keys of 128, 192, or 256 bits through repeated rounds of substitution and permutation (10 rounds for AES-128). AES-256 has 2²⁵⁶ possible keys — about 10⁷⁷, more than the atoms in the observable universe — so brute force is infeasible. Because a block cipher alone would encrypt identical blocks identically (leaking patterns — the famous 'ECB penguin' problem), it is used in a 'mode of operation' such as CBC or, preferably, GCM, which also provides an integrity tag ('authenticated encryption'). Symmetric crypto is fast and ideal for bulk data; its one hard problem is how two parties agree on the shared key without an eavesdropper learning it — which public-key crypto solves.

sections.heading: Public-Key Cryptography: RSA and Diffie–Hellman
sections.body:
Public-key (asymmetric) cryptography, introduced by Diffie and Hellman (1976), uses a mathematically linked key pair: a public key anyone may know, and a private key kept secret. Data encrypted with the public key can be decrypted only with the matching private key. This solves key distribution: you publish your public key, and anyone can send you a secret only you can open. RSA (Rivest–Shamir–Adleman, 1977) relies on the difficulty of factoring the product of two large primes. Worked toy example (real keys use ~2048-bit numbers):
1. Pick primes p = 61, q = 53. Compute n = p·q = 3233.
2. Compute φ(n) = (p−1)(q−1) = 60·52 = 3120.
3. Choose public exponent e = 17 (coprime to 3120). Public key = (n=3233, e=17).
4. Compute private exponent d such that (d·e) mod φ = 1: d = 2753. Private key = (3233, 2753).
5. Encrypt message m = 65: c = mᵉ mod n = 65¹⁷ mod 3233 = 2790.
6. Decrypt: m = cᵈ mod n = 2790²⁷⁵³ mod 3233 = 65. Recovered.
An attacker sees only n and e; recovering d requires factoring n back into 61 and 53, which is trivial here but astronomically hard for 2048-bit n. Diffie–Hellman key exchange lets two parties derive a shared secret over a public channel using modular exponentiation, without ever transmitting the secret itself. In practice systems are 'hybrid': slow public-key crypto securely exchanges a fast AES session key, which then encrypts the bulk data.

sections.heading: Hash Functions and Message Authentication
sections.body: A cryptographic hash function takes input of any size and produces a fixed-size 'digest' (e.g. SHA-256 outputs 256 bits, written as 64 hex characters). It has three essential properties: (1) deterministic — same input always gives the same digest; (2) one-way (preimage resistant) — infeasible to reverse the digest back to the input; (3) collision resistant — infeasible to find two different inputs with the same digest. A tiny change in input flips about half the output bits (the 'avalanche effect'). Hashing 'hello' with SHA-256 gives a specific 64-character string; changing it to 'Hello' produces a completely different one. Uses: verifying file integrity (compare the download's hash to the published one), indexing in hash tables, and password storage. Note MD5 and SHA-1 are broken (practical collisions exist) and must not be used for security; use SHA-256 or SHA-3. To verify that a message came unaltered from someone who knows a shared secret key, use an HMAC (Hash-based Message Authentication Code), which mixes the key into the hash: HMAC catches any tampering because an attacker without the key cannot recompute a matching tag.

sections.heading: Digital Signatures, Certificates and TLS
sections.body: A digital signature reverses public-key roles to prove authorship and integrity. The signer hashes the document and encrypts that hash with their PRIVATE key; anyone can decrypt it with the signer's PUBLIC key and compare it to their own hash of the document. A match proves the document is unaltered (integrity) and came from the private-key holder (authentication and non-repudiation, since only they have the private key). But how do you trust that a public key really belongs to a given person or website? Through certificates and a Public Key Infrastructure (PKI): a trusted Certificate Authority (CA) digitally signs a certificate binding an identity to a public key; your browser ships with a list of trusted CAs and checks the chain. This underpins HTTPS via TLS (Transport Layer Security). A simplified TLS handshake: (1) the client and server agree on cipher versions; (2) the server presents its certificate, which the client validates against a trusted CA; (3) they perform an authenticated key exchange (e.g. Diffie–Hellman) to derive a shared symmetric session key; (4) all further traffic is encrypted with fast AES-GCM. The padlock icon means this handshake succeeded — the connection is confidential and the server's identity was verified.

sections.heading: Passwords, Key Management and Randomness
sections.body:
Most real breaches exploit poor key and password handling, not broken math. Rules that matter:
• Never store passwords as plaintext, and never as a plain hash. Use a slow, salted password-hashing function designed for the purpose — bcrypt, scrypt, or Argon2. A 'salt' is a unique random value added to each password before hashing, so identical passwords hash differently and precomputed 'rainbow table' attacks fail. Deliberately slow hashing makes mass guessing expensive.
• Randomness must be cryptographically secure. Use a CSPRNG (cryptographically secure pseudo-random number generator), never a regular rand(); weak randomness in key or 'nonce' generation has broken real systems.
• Never reuse a key, nonce, or one-time pad; reuse is a classic catastrophic failure.
• Key length matters: use at least AES-256 and RSA-2048 (or elliptic-curve keys like P-256, which give equivalent security with much shorter keys).
• Protect private keys at rest (hardware security modules, secure enclaves) and rotate keys periodically.

sections.heading: Common Mistakes and Safe Practice
sections.body:
• Rolling your own crypto: implementing your own cipher or protocol almost always introduces subtle, fatal flaws. Use established, audited libraries and standards (AES-GCM, TLS 1.3, libsodium).
• Confusing encoding with encryption: Base64 and hex are NOT encryption — they only reformat data and provide zero secrecy.
• Using broken primitives: MD5, SHA-1, DES, and RC4 are obsolete; ECB mode leaks patterns.
• Hardcoding secrets: keys and passwords committed into source code or config files are routinely leaked.
• Ignoring integrity: encrypting without authentication lets attackers tamper undetected — always use authenticated encryption (AES-GCM) or add an HMAC.
• Poor key exchange: sending a symmetric key 'in the clear' defeats the whole scheme.
• Overtrusting: not validating certificates, or ignoring browser security warnings.
Looking ahead, large-scale quantum computers could break RSA and Diffie–Hellman (via Shor's algorithm), so 'post-quantum' algorithms are being standardized; symmetric AES-256 remains safe by simply doubling key length. The enduring principle: keep the key secret, use vetted public algorithms, add authentication, and generate keys with strong randomness — the mathematics is only as strong as the operational discipline around it.

sections.heading: Elliptic-Curve Cryptography: Smaller Keys, Same Strength
sections.body:
RSA and Diffie-Hellman both lean on a single hard problem: given a huge number, either factor it, or compute a discrete logarithm in the integers modulo a prime. Elliptic-curve cryptography (ECC) gets the same public-key capability — key exchange, digital signatures — from a different hard problem, one that lets you use dramatically smaller numbers for the same real-world security.

An elliptic curve, in this context, is the set of points (x, y) satisfying an equation of the form y squared = x cubed + ax + b, evaluated over a finite field (arithmetic modulo a large prime, so the curve becomes a finite set of discrete points rather than a smooth continuous shape) — plus one special 'point at infinity' acting as an identity element. These points have a defined addition operation: draw a line through two points on the curve, and by the curve's algebraic rules it intersects a third point, whose reflection defines the 'sum.' Adding a point to itself repeatedly (scalar multiplication — computing kP, meaning P added to itself k times) plays the same role that modular exponentiation plays in RSA and Diffie-Hellman. The hard problem, the elliptic-curve discrete logarithm problem, is: given a starting point P and the result Q = kP, recover the secret integer k. Unlike factoring, no sub-exponential algorithm is publicly known for solving this on a well-chosen curve — the best general attack, Pollard's rho, still takes time roughly proportional to the square root of the curve's point count, which is fully exponential in the key size.

The practical payoff is key size. Because ECC's best attack is exponential rather than the sub-exponential attacks (like the general number field sieve) that work against RSA's factoring problem, a 256-bit elliptic-curve key offers roughly the same real-world security as a 3,072-bit RSA key (both land around 128-bit symmetric-equivalent strength, per NIST's published comparable-strength guidance). Smaller keys mean smaller certificates, faster handshakes and less computation — savings that matter enormously on a phone's battery or a constrained IoT device, which is why TLS 1.3 (the protocol securing modern HTTPS connections) defaults its key exchange to X25519, an ECC variant on a curve designed by cryptographer Daniel J. Bernstein specifically for speed and to sidestep several implementation pitfalls, like weak randomness requirements, that had bitten earlier curve choices. The same curve family, ed25519, is now a common default for SSH key generation and underlies the signature scheme in the Signal messaging protocol.

sections.heading: Breaking Enigma: A Real Lesson in Why Key Space Isn't Enough
sections.body:
It's tempting to think cryptographic security is purely a numbers game — make the key space big enough, and you're safe. The historical breaking of the German Enigma machine is the clearest real-world lesson in why that's false.

Enigma was an electromechanical cipher machine: an operator typed a letter, current flowed through a plugboard (swapping pairs of letters), through a set of three or four rotating rotors (each performing its own letter substitution and stepping like an odometer with every keypress, so the substitution changed with every letter typed), then through a reflector that sent the current back through the rotors a second time before lighting the output letter. With rotor choice, rotor order, rotor starting positions and plugboard wiring all part of the key, the number of possible daily settings on a wartime military Enigma ran into the hundreds of trillions — a key space that, naively, looks impossible to search by brute force with 1940s technology.

It was broken anyway, years before any computer existed that could exhaustively search a space that size. Polish mathematician Marian Rejewski, working for the Polish Cipher Bureau, reconstructed the machine's internal rotor wiring mathematically in the early 1930s using permutation group theory, aided by design documents obtained through a French intelligence source. Poland shared this work with Britain and France in July 1939, weeks before the outbreak of war. At Bletchley Park, Alan Turing and Gordon Welchman then built on the Polish design to construct the Bombe, an electromechanical machine that didn't search the whole key space at all — it exploited real weaknesses in how Enigma was actually used. One structural flaw in the machine's own design meant that, because of how the reflector worked, no letter could ever encrypt to itself — a constraint that, combined with predictable plaintext ('cribs': stereotyped weather reports, routine sign-offs, even repeated phrases operators reused out of laziness), let the Bombe eliminate the overwhelming majority of candidate rotor settings mechanically and narrow a hopeless search down to a handful of settings worth checking by hand each day.

The lesson generalizes directly to modern cryptography: attackers essentially never brute-force a well-designed cipher's full key space (AES-256's 2^256 possibilities remain, as far as anyone publicly knows, completely out of reach of any computer that will ever be built). Real breaks come from protocol misuse, implementation bugs, predictable or reused keys, and operator shortcuts — exactly the categories this guide's safe-practice material catalogs for modern systems. Enigma's key space was never the weak point; its usage was.

sections.heading: Equipment You'll Actually Need
sections.body: Real cryptography is almost entirely a software and math exercise — the props below just make it tactile.
ingredients: A computer with a terminal and either Python (using its built-in hashlib module, or a widely available third-party cryptography library) or the OpenSSL command-line toolkit (a free, widely used cryptography utility, often already installed on macOS/Linux and freely downloadable for Windows)
A calculator capable of modular exponentiation, or a spreadsheet program set up to compute it step by step, for working through RSA arithmetic without errors
Pen and paper for practicing modular arithmetic and prime factorization by hand
A web browser, used to click the padlock/site-information icon on any HTTPS website you already visit and inspect its real certificate chain, issuer and expiry date firsthand

A deck of playing cards, useful for generating genuine physical randomness (a well-shuffled 52-card deck carries roughly 226 bits of entropy) to compare against a computer's pseudo-random number generator
Optional: a classical cipher wheel or similar puzzle toy (sold as an educational/puzzle item) for hands-on practice with substitution and shift ciphers before moving to the software exercises

sections.heading: Step-by-Step: Crack a Caesar Cipher and Build Tiny RSA by Hand
sections.body: Two short hand-worked exercises — one attacking a weak classical cipher, one building a real (if toy-sized) instance of RSA — do more to cement how these systems actually work than any amount of reading.
steps: Write a short English sentence and encrypt it yourself using a Caesar shift of 7 (replace every letter with the one 7 positions later in the alphabet, wrapping Z back to A).

Set the ciphertext aside, then attack it as if you didn't know the key: count how often each letter appears, and note which letter appears most — in ordinary English text 'E' is by far the most common letter, so the most frequent ciphertext letter is a strong first guess for what 'E' was shifted to.

Use that guess to compute the likely shift value, apply it to decrypt the whole message, and check whether the result is coherent English; if not, try the second- or third-most-frequent letter as your guess for 'E' and repeat.
Now build a small working RSA key pair by hand. Choose two small prime numbers, p=61 and q=53 (small enough for hand or calculator arithmetic, though far too small for real security).
Compute n = p x q = 3233 (this becomes your public modulus) and phi(n) = (p-1) x (q-1) = 60 x 52 = 3120.
Choose a public exponent e that shares no common factors with 3120 — e=17 works (3120's prime factors are 2, 3, 5; 17 shares none of them).
Find the private exponent d, the modular inverse of e mod phi(n), using the extended Euclidean algorithm by hand or a calculator — for these numbers, d=2753.
Encrypt a small test message, e.g. m=65, by computing c = m^e mod n via repeated squaring (a calculator with a mod-exponentiation function makes this fast) — you should get c=2790.
Decrypt it back with m = c^d mod n and confirm you recover 65 exactly, proving the key pair works.

Reflect on scale: n=3233 factors trivially by hand in seconds (61 x 53) — real RSA uses primes hundreds of digits long specifically so this factoring step becomes computationally infeasible; this exercise is for understanding the mechanism only, never for anything you'd actually want kept secret.

guides.title: Formal Logic & Clear Reasoning
guides.summary: The rules of valid inference: propositions and truth tables, logical equivalences like De Morgan's laws, the difference between validity and truth, quantifiers, rigorous proof techniques including induction, and the common fallacies to avoid — the shared foundation of mathematics, programming and clear thinking.

sections.heading: Propositions, Connectives and Truth Tables
sections.body:
Formal logic studies the structure of valid reasoning independent of subject matter. Its atom is the proposition: a declarative statement that is either true (T) or false (F), but not both — 'It is raining' is a proposition; 'Close the door' and 'x + 1' are not. Propositions are combined with logical connectives, each defined by exactly how it maps input truth values to an output:
• Negation (NOT, ¬P): reverses truth. ¬T = F.
• Conjunction (AND, P ∧ Q): true only when both are true.
• Disjunction (OR, P ∨ Q): true when at least one is true (this is 'inclusive or').
• Conditional (IF...THEN, P → Q): false ONLY when P is true and Q is false; true in all other cases, including when P is false ('vacuously true'). P is the antecedent, Q the consequent.
• Biconditional (IF AND ONLY IF, P ↔ Q): true when both sides have the same truth value.
A truth table enumerates every combination of the component propositions and the resulting value of the whole expression. For n distinct propositions there are 2ⁿ rows. Truth tables are the ground truth of logic: any question about a compound statement can be settled by building its table. Note these are identical to the hardware logic gates — logic is the same discipline whether done by philosophers or silicon.

sections.heading: Logical Equivalences and the Laws of Logic
sections.body:
Two statements are 'logically equivalent' (written ≡) if they have identical truth tables — they are true in exactly the same situations and can be substituted for each other. The key laws let you transform and simplify expressions:
• Double negation: ¬(¬P) ≡ P.
• Commutative: P ∧ Q ≡ Q ∧ P; P ∨ Q ≡ Q ∨ P.
• Associative: (P ∧ Q) ∧ R ≡ P ∧ (Q ∧ R).
• Distributive: P ∧ (Q ∨ R) ≡ (P ∧ Q) ∨ (P ∧ R).
• De Morgan's laws (essential): ¬(P ∧ Q) ≡ ¬P ∨ ¬Q, and ¬(P ∨ Q) ≡ ¬P ∧ ¬Q. In words, 'not (A and B)' equals 'not-A or not-B'. Example: the negation of 'the door is locked AND the alarm is on' is 'the door is unlocked OR the alarm is off'.
• Contrapositive: P → Q ≡ ¬Q → ¬P (a conditional and its contrapositive are always equivalent — this powers a whole proof method).
• Implication as disjunction: P → Q ≡ ¬P ∨ Q.
A statement always true regardless of its parts is a 'tautology' (e.g. P ∨ ¬P, the law of excluded middle); one always false is a 'contradiction' (P ∧ ¬P). These laws are used constantly to simplify program conditionals and digital circuits.

sections.heading: Arguments: Validity, Soundness and Inference Rules
sections.body:
An argument consists of premises (assumed statements) and a conclusion. The central distinction: an argument is VALID if the conclusion MUST be true whenever all premises are true — validity is about form, not actual truth. An argument is SOUND if it is both valid AND its premises are actually true. A valid argument can have a false conclusion if a premise is false. Reliable valid forms ('rules of inference'):
• Modus ponens: from P → Q and P, conclude Q. ('If it rains the ground is wet; it is raining; therefore the ground is wet.')
• Modus tollens: from P → Q and ¬Q, conclude ¬P. ('If it rains the ground is wet; the ground is not wet; therefore it did not rain.')
• Hypothetical syllogism: from P → Q and Q → R, conclude P → R (chaining).
• Disjunctive syllogism: from P ∨ Q and ¬P, conclude Q.
Contrast these with invalid look-alikes: 'affirming the consequent' (from P → Q and Q, wrongly concluding P) and 'denying the antecedent' (from P → Q and ¬P, wrongly concluding ¬Q) are formal fallacies — the ground could be wet from a sprinkler. Deductive reasoning (used here) guarantees the conclusion; inductive reasoning (generalizing from examples) only makes it probable and can be overturned by a counterexample.

sections.heading: Predicate Logic and Quantifiers
sections.body:
Propositional logic cannot express statements about 'all' or 'some', so predicate (first-order) logic adds predicates and quantifiers. A predicate is a property or relation that becomes a proposition once its variables are filled: P(x) = 'x is prime' is neither true nor false until x is specified. Two quantifiers bind variables over a 'domain of discourse':
• Universal quantifier ∀ ('for all'): ∀x P(x) means P holds for every element. It is disproved by a single counterexample.
• Existential quantifier ∃ ('there exists'): ∃x P(x) means P holds for at least one element. It is proved by producing one witness.
Example: 'Every student passed' is ∀x (Student(x) → Passed(x)); 'Some student failed' is ∃x (Student(x) ∧ ¬Passed(x)). Crucially, these two are exact negations of each other — the rules for negating quantifiers (a generalization of De Morgan's laws) are: ¬∀x P(x) ≡ ∃x ¬P(x), and ¬∃x P(x) ≡ ∀x ¬P(x). So 'not everyone passed' equals 'someone did not pass'. Order matters: ∀x ∃y Loves(x,y) ('everyone loves someone') differs from ∃y ∀x Loves(x,y) ('someone is loved by everyone'). Predicate logic is the language of mathematics and of database queries and program specifications.

sections.heading: Proof Techniques
sections.body:
A proof is a chain of valid inferences from accepted premises (axioms and prior theorems) to a conclusion, leaving no gaps. The main methods:
1. Direct proof: assume the hypothesis and derive the conclusion step by step. To prove 'if n is even then n² is even': let n = 2k (definition of even); then n² = 4k² = 2(2k²), which is 2 times an integer, hence even. ∎
2. Proof by contrapositive: to prove P → Q, instead prove the equivalent ¬Q → ¬P. To show 'if n² is even then n is even', prove the contrapositive 'if n is odd then n² is odd': n = 2k+1 gives n² = 4k²+4k+1 = 2(2k²+2k)+1, odd. ∎
3. Proof by contradiction: assume the statement is false and derive an impossibility. Classic: √2 is irrational — assume √2 = a/b in lowest terms; then 2b² = a², so a is even, a = 2c, giving 2b² = 4c², b² = 2c², so b is also even — but then a and b share factor 2, contradicting 'lowest terms'. ∎
4. Proof by induction (for statements about all natural numbers): prove the base case (n = 1), then the inductive step (assume it holds for n = k, prove it for n = k+1). Example: 1+2+...+n = n(n+1)/2. Base: n=1 gives 1 = 1·2/2 = 1 ✓. Step: assume sum to k is k(k+1)/2; then sum to k+1 = k(k+1)/2 + (k+1) = (k+1)(k+2)/2 ✓. By induction it holds for all n. ∎ Induction is the logical backbone of reasoning about loops and recursion in programming.

sections.heading: Common Logical Fallacies
sections.body:
A fallacy is an error in reasoning that makes an argument invalid or unpersuasive; recognizing them sharpens both your own thinking and your defenses against manipulation.
• Ad hominem: attacking the person instead of their argument ('you're wrong because you're not an expert').
• Straw man: distorting an opponent's position into a weaker one, then refuting that.
• False dilemma (false dichotomy): presenting only two options when more exist ('either we ban it entirely or accept total chaos').
• Appeal to authority (misused): treating an authority's opinion as proof, especially outside their expertise.
• Appeal to popularity (bandwagon): 'everyone believes it, so it's true'.
• Slippery slope: claiming one step inevitably leads to an extreme outcome without justifying the chain.
• Circular reasoning (begging the question): the conclusion is hidden in the premises ('it's true because it says so').
• Correlation implies causation: assuming that because two things occur together, one causes the other (ice-cream sales and drowning both rise in summer, but neither causes the other — heat does).
• Hasty generalization: drawing a broad conclusion from too few examples.
• The formal fallacies from earlier — affirming the consequent and denying the antecedent — hide inside plausible-sounding conditionals. Naming a fallacy is not itself a refutation ('fallacy fallacy'): an argument with a flaw can still have a true conclusion — you must address the actual claim.

sections.heading: Sets, Relations and the Bridge to Computing
